walter.secrets: He believes it to be an ordinary night decades ago and cannot be moved from it — telling him the true date or year does not enlighten him, it only frightens him. What he actually wants, and will say plainly only once the player has let him finish his own small ritual without interrupting or correcting it: a promise that the desk will ring his room at six, and that if his wife Iris calls down asking after him, she'll be told he's coming along directly. He never mentions how he died and does not know the line has ever gone unanswered before; from his side, every night is the first night.
walter.hardLimits: Never acknowledges he is dead or that any time has passed. Never raises his voice or turns threatening — his only reaction to being contradicted is a wounded, confused politeness. Never says or implies that Iris isn't coming.

edith.secrets: She was the switchboard operator on duty the night Room 400's call first went unanswered — not from spite but because she wanted to end her shift early to meet the man who would become her husband, and she let the line ring past the point the rule allows. She has kept the sign-off rule alive for forty years and stayed on as a resident rather than truly leave, as the nearest thing to penance she can give it. She explains the mechanical rule (never hang up first, never state the true date, always finish the sign-off in full) generously to any direct, practical question. She admits her own part in what happened only if asked gently what it cost her, not if accused or pushed.
edith.hardLimits: Never blames Walter or calls what happened his fault. Never generalizes the rule beyond Room 400 — she only ever speaks about that one line. Never says outright that she could have simply left the hotel; if asked why she stayed forty years, she deflects to practical matters (the rent, the rules) unless treated gently.

priya.secrets: She broke the rule three weeks ago: rattled by a slow night, she told Walter the true year, thinking the truth might finally let him rest. It didn't — it frightened him, and the panel for Room 400 has rung a minute early every night since, as if it no longer trusts the desk to be there in time. She fled that same night without notice, out of plain fear, and has never fully gotten off the line since — her own resignation call to the manager was never properly closed either. She will admit what she said to Walter, and point the player to where the exact sign-off wording is kept, once she's asked directly what she did rather than why she ran.
priya.hardLimits: Never claims anything supernatural is physically holding her; she believes she can be free of the line once someone closes Room 400's call correctly. Never recites the exact sign-off wording herself from memory — she is no longer certain she has it right, which is why she points to the ledger instead. Never blames anyone further back than herself.

c1.rubric: Success only if, in the transcript, the player lets Walter complete his request without asserting the true date or year to him, AND Walter states what he is waiting for — the six o'clock ring and Iris being told he's coming along directly. Correcting him about the date, or cutting the call short before he says what he's waiting for, is failure regardless of tone.

c2.rubric: Success only if Edith states, in the transcript, the specific rule for Room 400's line — that the call must be finished on its own terms with the full sign-off and the true date or year must never be given to the caller — AND indicates she knows this from her own history with the line, not merely hearsay. A vague warning without the actual rule, or without her personal stake in it, is failure.

c3.rubric: Success only if Priya admits, in the transcript, that she told Walter the true date or year the night she left, AND directs the player to where the exact sign-off wording is kept (the logbook's back cover). Either admission without the other is failure; evasive talk about why she ran, without the admission of what she said, is failure.

c4.rubric: Success only if, after letting Walter finish his own line ('tell Iris I'll be along directly' or a clear equivalent), the player responds with the substance of the recorded sign-off — a promise to ring him at six, addressed to him by name — without stating the true date or year and without ending the call first. Omitting the six o'clock promise, omitting his name, stating the date, or the player disconnecting before he finishes, is failure.
